The average two-bedroom rent in the Toronto CMA was **$2,045 a month** in the October 2025 CMHC Rental Market Survey. That is **$73 (about 3.7%) higher** than the $1,972 in October 2024.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 34-10-0133-01, vector **v3823103**. The series is Toronto, Ontario; row and apartment structures of three units and over; two-bedroom units.
- **Reference periods:** StatCan labels the survey by year, so the 2025 value is October 2025 and the 2024 value is October 2024. The table was released 2025-12-17.
- **Units:** The values are nominal dollars, not adjusted for inflation. The percentage change is my own calculation from the two published values.
- **Scope:** CMHC's average rent is what tenants actually pay across occupied and vacant units. It is not an asking rent.

The Toronto CMA purpose-built rental vacancy rate was **3.0% in October 2025**, up from **1.4% in October 2023**. That is a rise of 1.6 percentage points, so the rate is a bit more than double its 2023 level.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 34-10-0130-01, vector v1930324. The data are CMHC's Rental Market Survey, taken in October each year. The table covers privately initiated row and apartment structures of three or more units, weighted average.
- **2024:** the rate was 2.5%, so the increase has been steady across the period.
- **Other table:** 34-10-0127-01 covers only apartment structures of six or more units. Its rates differ, and I did not pull it.
- **Release:** the 2025 figure was published 2025-12-17. The table has no later reference period, and I did not check for revisions.

In the October 2025 CMHC Rental Market Survey, the average two-bedroom rent in the Oshawa CMA was **$1,762**, which is **$283 (about 14%) lower** than Toronto's **$2,045**.

| CMA | 2025 avg. 2-bed rent | 2024 | Change 2024–25 | Vector |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oshawa | $1,762 | $1,690 | +4.3% | v3823091 |
| Toronto | $2,045 | $1,972 | +3.7% | v3823103 |

- **Gap:** Oshawa's rent was about 86% of Toronto's. The gap was slightly narrower than in 2024, when it was $282, or 14.3%.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 34-10-0133-01, which republishes CMHC data. Both series cover row and apartment structures of three or more units. The reference period is October 2025, released 2025-12-17.
- **Quality:** Both values carry normal status, with no data-quality flags.
- **Caveats:** Rents are in current dollars. The change figures are my own calculation from the published averages, not CMHC's same-structure percent change.

**Oshawa** had the highest rental vacancy rate of the three in 2025.

| CMA | Vacancy rate, Oct 2025 | Vector |
|---|---|---|
| Oshawa | 3.6% | v1930312 |
| Hamilton | 3.5% | v1930306 |
| Toronto | 3.0% | v1930324 |

- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 34-10-0130-01, which republishes the CMHC Rental Market Survey. It covers row and apartment structures of three units and over, as a weighted average. The reference period is 2025, with the survey taken in October.
- **Margin:** Oshawa and Hamilton are only 0.1 percentage points apart. I didn't check CMHC's reliability flags, so I can't say whether that gap is statistically meaningful.
- **Table choice:** The six-units-and-over table (34-10-0127-01) uses a narrower universe, so its rates differ. I didn't pull those figures.

I've pulled Toronto CMA housing starts from the monthly and annual StatCan tables, and I'm giving the comparison now.

**Toronto CMA housing starts, total units**

| Year | Starts | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 | **26,087** | Table 34-10-0154-01, vector v42127475, Jan–Dec 2025 monthly values summed. This matches the annual table 34-10-0134-01, vector v42127955, for 2025. |
| 2024 | **37,718** | Table 34-10-0154-01, vector v42127475, Jan–Dec 2024 monthly values summed. |

**Comparison:** 2025 was 11,631 units lower than 2024, a drop of about 30.8%.

**Caveats:**
- The 2024 total is my own sum of the 12 monthly values. The annual table 34-10-0134-01 returns no value for 2024, so I couldn't check the 2024 total against a published annual figure.
- The 2025 sum matches the published annual figure, which suggests the monthly values add up correctly.
- The source is the CMHC Starts and Completions Survey, published through StatCan. StatCan notes that CMA boundaries change every five years, so comparisons across census-definition changes aren't strictly like-for-like.

New home prices in the Toronto CMA fell about 3.4% between December 2024 and December 2025.

| Reference period | New Housing Price Index, total (house and land), 201612=100 |
|---|---|
| December 2024 | 113.1 |
| December 2025 | 109.3 |

- **Change:** −3.8 index points, which is −3.4% (my calculation from the two published values).
- **Trend:** the index declined in most months of 2025. It was 112.6 in January and 109.4 in both October and November.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada table 18-10-0205-01, vector v111955499 ("Toronto, Ontario; Total (house and land)"). Both values are normal-quality, with no flags.
- **What it measures:** this is an index of contractor-reported selling prices for new homes, not an average dollar price.

A year of average two-bedroom rent in Toronto in 2024 would take about **61% of the median after-tax income**.

- **Rent:** The 2024 average two-bedroom rent in the Toronto CMA was $1,972 a month, or $23,664 a year. This is table 34-10-0133-01, vector v3823103, from the CMHC survey taken in October 2024. It covers row and apartment structures of three or more units.
- **Income:** The median after-tax income was $38,600. This is table 11-10-0238-01, vector v107657424, for 2024. Its unit is 2024 constant dollars, which equal current dollars for that year, so the two figures can be compared directly.
- **Share:** $23,664 ÷ $38,600 ≈ 61.3%. I calculated this myself from the two figures.

**Caveats**
- The income figure is for individuals aged 15 and over, not households or families. A household's median income is higher, so the share for a household would be lower. The CMA-level household and family figures are in table 11-10-0237-01. I did not pull them.
- The rent is the average for all occupied and vacant units in the surveyed structures, not asking rents. It does not cover condos or other rentals outside that survey.
- The rent is an October snapshot and the income is for the calendar year, so the periods only roughly line up.

Over 2019–2024, average two-bedroom rent in the Toronto CMA rose about 26%, while median after-tax income rose about 2%.

| Measure | 2019 | 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average two-bedroom rent, Toronto CMA, row and apartment structures of 3+ units (monthly) | $1,563 | $1,972 | **+26.2%** |
| Median after-tax income, Toronto CMA, economic families and persons not in an economic family | $80,800 | $82,500 | **+2.1%** |

- **Rent source:** Table 34-10-0133-01, vector v3823103. It is CMHC's October Rental Market Survey, in current dollars. The change is the gap between two years' averages. CMHC's own like-for-like percent change would differ somewhat, and I did not pull it.
- **Income source:** Table 11-10-0237-01, vector v107655746. The 2024 estimate is rated "excellent" quality, and 2019 is rated "very good".
- **Income units:** The table's unit code (455) suggests constant (inflation-adjusted) dollars, but I could not confirm this. Rent is in current dollars, so the two growth rates may not be on the same price basis. Check the table's unit before treating the gap as exact.
- **Income definition:** The figure covers all economic families plus unattached individuals. It is not renter-specific or two-bedroom-household income.
- **Other income tables:** The CMA table that mentions after-tax income (11-10-0035-01) is archived and only covers 2012. Table 11-10-0009-01 reports median total income, not after-tax.

In Toronto, the 2025 average two-bedroom rent equals about **25.3% of 2021 Census median household income**.

- **Rent:** $2,045 a month, or $24,540 a year. This is the CMHC Rental Market Survey average for two-bedroom units in row and apartment structures of three or more units, Toronto CMA, October 2025. Source: StatCan table 34-10-0133-01, vector v3823103, reference period 2025.
- **Income:** $97,000. This is the median total household income in 2020 for the Toronto CMA, from the 2021 Census Profile (characteristic 229, released 2022-07-13). The Census Profile has no StatCan vector ID, and StatCan randomly rounds census values. The income year is 2020, so it predates the rent year by five years.

The calculation is $24,540 ÷ $97,000 ≈ 25.3%.

**Caveats:**
- The ratio mixes 2025 rent with 2020 income, so it overstates the burden today. Incomes have grown since 2020.
- The rent is an average for purpose-built rentals, not asking rents. It is not what a new tenant would pay today.
- Median household income covers all households. Renter households typically have lower incomes, so their rent burden would be higher than this figure.

Toronto rents rose faster than overall prices in 2025. Rented accommodation inflation was about 3.1%, against about 1.8% for all items. Both figures are calendar-2025 annual averages, from Statistics Canada table 18-10-0005-01 (CPI, annual average, not seasonally adjusted).

| Toronto series | Vector | 2024 index | 2025 index | 2025 inflation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rented accommodation | v41695188 | 158.6 | 163.5 | **3.1%** |
| All-items | v41695186 | 164.7 | 167.7 | **1.8%** |

The indexes are on a 2002=100 base. I calculated the percentage changes myself from the published, rounded annual averages, so they can differ by about 0.1 point from any rate Statistics Canada publishes directly.

I have both series, so here's the comparison.

**Shelter CPI, 2025 annual average vs 2024 (table 18-10-0005-01, not seasonally adjusted, 2002=100)**

| | 2024 | 2025 | 2025 inflation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Toronto (v41695187) | 187.3 | 191.3 | **2.1%** |
| Canada (v41693348) | 182.3 | 187.8 | **3.0%** |

Toronto's shelter inflation in 2025 was about 0.9 percentage points below the national rate. Both cooled from 2024, when Toronto was at 5.9% and Canada at 5.7%. That makes Toronto the one that went from slightly above Canada to well below it.

- **Method:** These are calendar-year changes between annual average indexes. I computed them from the published, rounded index values, so they could differ by 0.1 point from a figure calculated another way. They are not December-to-December changes.
- **Components:** I did not break shelter into rent, owned accommodation or mortgage interest. Mortgage interest cost is published for Canada only, so there is no Toronto figure for it.

I pulled the August 2026 Toronto CPI figures, so here is the comparison.

In August 2026, Toronto shelter prices were slightly lower than a year earlier, while overall consumer prices were higher.

| Toronto, August 2026 | Index (2002=100) | Year over year |
|---|---|---|
| Shelter (v41692889) | 190.5 | **-0.5%** |
| All-items (v41692888) | 171.7 | **+2.1%** |

- **Gap:** Shelter was about 2.6 percentage points below overall inflation.
- **Source:** Both series come from Statistics Canada table 18-10-0004-01 (CPI, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), reference period August 2026.
- **Calculation:** I calculated the year-over-year changes from the published index levels as 100 × (August 2026 ÷ August 2025 − 1). Statistics Canada doesn't publish them directly in this table. Both figures are rounded.
- **Latest data:** September 2026 is already out. Shelter was -0.3% and all-items +2.1% year over year in that month.

I can also break shelter into rented and owned accommodation for Toronto, which this table does publish.

The Bank of Canada changed its policy rate **4 times in 2025**. Each change was a 25-basis-point cut.

The rate started 2025 at **3.25%** and ended it at **2.25%**, a total of 100 basis points lower.

| Effective date | Rate after change |
|---|---|
| 2025-01-30 | 3.00% |
| 2025-03-13 | 2.75% |
| 2025-09-18 | 2.50% |
| 2025-10-30 | 2.25% |

The rate was unchanged at 2.75% from March through mid-September.

The 3.25% starting level came from the December 2024 cut. The rate was 3.75% until 2024-12-11 and fell to 3.25% on 2024-12-12.

The 2025 rate on each date in the table is the Bank of Canada Valet series V39079, "Target for the overnight rate" (business daily). The reference period is 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31.

This is Bank of Canada data, not Statistics Canada, so there is no StatCan table or vector ID.

There is no Toronto figure for mortgage interest cost inflation. Statistics Canada publishes that CPI component for Canada only, not for any city or province. For Toronto, tables 18-10-0004 and 18-10-0005 carry only six series: all-items, shelter, rented accommodation, owned accommodation, water/fuel/electricity, and all-items (1992=100).

**National figure (Canada), the closest available:**
- Mortgage interest cost CPI rose **5.3%** in 2025 on an annual-average basis.
- The index went from 173.2 in 2024 to 182.4 in 2025 (2002=100).
- Source: table 18-10-0005-01, vector v41693354, reference period calendar year 2025.
- I calculated the 5.3% from the published, rounded annual indexes. Statistics Canada does not publish this percentage itself.
- For comparison, the same series rose 20.1% in 2024 and 28.5% in 2023, so 2025 was a sharp slowdown.

If you want a Toronto-specific measure, I can pull the Toronto shelter or owned accommodation CPI, but those don't isolate mortgage interest.

It starts in 1987, so it has nothing for 1985. The related vacancy-rate table, 34-10-0130-01, starts in 1992. The earliest figure available is the 1987 value in table 34-10-0133-01. I haven't pulled it. I can fetch the 1987 two-bedroom Toronto figure and its vector ID if that's useful. A 1985 number might exist in CMHC's print publications from that period, but I couldn't verify one here.
